The material has five kinds of documents, and each answers a different question about the claudetto rebuild.

The first is the map, which is `README.md`. It defines the plan's layout, the eleven blocks (kernel, guards, handover, delegation, reply, cost, setup, edit, openspec, you-should-know, verification), the routing rules that decide which file an item belongs in, the item format with its ID prefixes, the attribution forms, and the audit of sources. Its job is to tell a reader where everything lives and how each claim must be sourced.

The second is the goal statement, `goal.md`. It says what the rebuild must produce: three plugins on a vanilla Claude Code 2.1.327 install, with handover replacing auto compaction, disables for `@builtin` plugins, a perl batch edit tool, and the medical-error approach to agent faults. It also lists the working rules (probe before relying on a fact, always cite a source, ask through `AskUserQuestion`, no benchmarks, no hyphenated file families) and the definition of done.

The third is the architecture decision records under `adr/`, in MADR 4.0.0 form with one decision per file. Each records a context, the options considered, the chosen outcome, the consequences, and a source, plus a status such as accepted or superseded. They explain why a design was chosen, and they keep superseded choices visible. The ones shown cover settings choices (auto mode, model family, agent view), the Monitor tool saga, user conduct rules (agent does the work itself, asks through `AskUserQuestion`, commits when allowed, holds releases until told), and the Stop grader and hook fault policy.

The fourth, described in the README but not included in this material, is the product requirements set under `prd/`. These are individual requirements with acceptance checks, status at the baseline commit, and sources, following ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148. Alongside them are the arc42 sections covering constraints, context, runtime algorithms, concepts, and quality scenarios.

The fifth, also described but not included, is the risk register under `risk-register/<block>.md`. Each entry treats an agent failure as a medical error with a cause, likelihood, impact, and cure, following ISO 31000 fields. A reference copy of the you-should-know prompt rounds out the set.

END-OF-REPLY

The risk register itself is not in this material, so these come from the ADRs, the README's audit notes, and the goal.

The most serious is the silent loss of auto mode's safety review. ADR-0025 records that on Claude Code 2.1.319, and again on 2.1.327, a hook that rewrites a tool's input sets `serverClassifierInputRewritten`, so every call in that response comes back with "gave no verdict". That is why claudetto denies with the exact form instead of rewriting. A related risk is that gating hooks fail open. ADR-0035 reports that 64 of 92 catch blocks bound no error and hid defects, and that a bare catch turned a bad grader answer into a clean reply. A guard with no catch lets a throw or a 10-second overrun through. That policy was later superseded, but the risk it describes is a real one for any hook that gates a call.

A third risk is destructive tooling. ADR-0036 notes that `oxlint --fix-suggestions` deleted 81 `console.log` calls and removed `async` from 8 functions, which was reproduced. That is the "user work lost" kind of impact the README rates at 4. Fourth is prompt injection against the permission decider. ADR-0017 says Jev may deny or ask but never allow, because jevwire is not hardened against injection, so an injected text cannot open a gate.

Fifth is the loss of evidence behind the plan. The README says session logs from 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-16 are no longer on disk, so citations to them survive only through git history. It also says 145 items have a source line that was not found, and 13 items were removed because no source could be located. The audit limits add to this: some batches matched by keyword only, and early Haiku search workers thrashed.

Sixth is drift between what is installed and what is in the source. ADR-0027 records that the installed plugin still allowed reads the source now denied, and the user accepts no such gap, so the branch plugin must be loaded at once with `--plugin-dir`. Finally, cost and conduct run through the whole set. Examples are the auto-mode classifier cost, Monitor's 7,588-character stock definition, Mythos model prices, and paid evals needing approval. On the conduct side, the agent deferring steps it could run itself, or asking in plain text instead of through `AskUserQuestion`, is treated as a fault to cure with a general fix.

END-OF-REPLY

Start by reading the map. `plans/rebuild/README.md` explains the layout, the eleven blocks, the routing rules, the item format and the attribution forms. Then read `prd/README.md` for purpose, scope and what is out, followed by the `prd/<block>.md` file for whichever block you will build first. Alongside it, read `arc42/02_architecture_constraints/`, `arc42/06_runtime_view/`, the relevant `adr/` records and `risk-register/<block>.md`, so you know the limits, the algorithms, why each choice was made, and which agent faults to guard against. Superseded ADRs are kept on purpose, so check each record's status before relying on it.

Next, set up the working environment. Work on the branch `feat/claudetto-2.1.325-reinstantiation` against a vanilla Claude Code 2.1.327 install. Per ADR-0027, load the branch's plugin with `--plugin-dir` and keep any installed copy disabled, so a fix is live in the session that made it.

Then pick the work by its checkboxes. Each `- [ ]` item in `plans/rebuild/` carries an acceptance check, a verification method, and a status of have, partial or missing at baseline `088a227c`, so start with items marked missing in a block that others depend on. The kernel block is the natural first candidate, since the other blocks build on its hooks. For each item, probe `claude` 2.1.327 to confirm any fact you rely on, and record the probe name, version, date and command as the attribution. Build the smallest change that meets the acceptance check, keeping files small, split by concern, and free of hyphenated families such as `foo.ts` and `foo-one.ts`.

Tick an item only when its acceptance check passes, and name the command and its result in the commit. Commit your own work as separate Conventional Commits (ADR-0030). Whenever the user alone holds an answer, including what is worthwhile against vanilla 2.1.327, ask through `AskUserQuestion` rather than guessing. When you hit a new agent fault, record it as a medical error in `risk-register/<block>.md` and cure it with one general fix across subsystems, not a one-off patch.

Finally, dogfood. Install claudetto on the vanilla install, use it on itself, and fix what that shows, repeating until nothing is left to align. The plan is finished when every checkbox is ticked or moved to scope Out with a reason, `claude plugin test` passes, and a dogfood session shows no open risk-register item at Likelihood 3 or higher. Per ADR-0032, do not merge, tag or release until the user says go.

END-OF-REPLY

The risk-register files themselves are not in the material, so these come from the README, `goal.md`, and the ADRs, which record the risks that shaped each decision.

The most consequential technical risk is that rewriting a tool's input voids auto mode's server review. ADR-0025 records that in 2.1.319 a changed input sets `serverClassifierInputRewritten`, and every call in that response comes back "gave no verdict". That is why claudetto denies with the exact form instead of rewriting, and why ADR-0037 refuses a hook that sets default isolation on agent calls. A related risk is hook failure: ADR-0035 notes that 64 of 92 catches bound no error and hid defects, and that a bare catch turned a bad grader answer into a clean reply. Whether a fault fails open or asks a person is a real safety question, and that ADR was later superseded by ADR-0168.

A second group is unsafe automation damaging user work. ADR-0036 records a reproduced case where `oxlint --fix-suggestions` deleted 81 `console.log` calls and removed `async` from 8 functions. ADR-0017 keeps Jev from ever allowing a permission, because jevwire is not hardened against injection and an injected text could otherwise open a gate. ADR-0041 records the opposite failure: the old time-cap hook refused 43 calls from agents that were still making progress.

A third group is agent conduct, which `goal.md` tells the work to treat as medical errors with general cures. The ADRs show several of them. The agent cited rule files and dossiers it had not read (ADR-0028 and ADR-0029). It handed doable steps back to the user (ADR-0042). It reported and waited after a correction instead of fixing (ADR-0044). It also set a requested value on a claim the workspace could not check (ADR-0013). Each costs a wasted turn or session, and an unchecked claim can ship a wrong result.

A fourth group is cost and spend. ADR-0005 limits sessions to the -5-5 model family because Mythos models cost too much. ADR-0003 and ADR-0031 weigh tool-text bytes against features, with stock Monitor at 7,588 characters. ADR-0039 shows a paid eval cap of $20 that was the agent's own figure, not the user's, and ADR-0019 shows a weekly paid-work cap that was later dropped.

The last group is the plan's own evidence base, which the README admits is partly lost. Session logs from 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-16 are no longer on disk, 145 items have source lines that were not found, and 13 items were removed because no source could be located. Several audit batches matched by keyword only, and some version claims were checked by a grep of release notes rather than a probe. This matters because `goal.md` requires every fact to be verified by a probe against 2.1.327, so stale or unverifiable items could carry wrong requirements into the rebuild.

Smaller risks also appear: a gap between the installed plugin and the branch source (ADR-0027), and silent truncation of skill descriptions past the listing cap (ADR-0023).

END-OF-REPLY

The material is a plan for rebuilding claudetto, split into document kinds that each answer one question. No bullets here, so I'll walk through them in prose.

The top-level files are the README, which is the map (layout, routing rules, item format, attribution forms, audit counts), and goal.md, which is the prompt that tells an agent what to rebuild, the rules it must follow, and what "done" means.

The PRD (prd/) holds the product requirements in the outline of ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148. Its README states purpose, scope (including a long "Out" list of things that are dropped, each with a reason), product perspective, assumptions, and deferred work. One file per block (kernel, guards, handover, delegation, reply, cost, setup, edit, openspec, you-should-know, verification) then holds the individual requirements, each with an acceptance check, a verification method, a basis and a status at the baseline commit.

The ADRs (adr/) are architecture decision records in MADR format, one decision per file. They record why a design was chosen, which options were considered, and what the consequences are, and they mark which decisions were superseded by later ones. Most trace to a user decision or a measurement.

The arc42 sections describe the architecture. Section 1 gives goals and stakeholders. Section 2 lists fixed constraints (sandbox limits, user rules, rebuild rules, eval integrity). Section 3 holds measured or documented facts about Claude Code 2.1.327 and the machine: settings, hooks, tools, cache, cost, models, and so on. Section 4 is the solution strategy. Section 5 is the building block view of what exists at baseline 088a227c. Section 6 is the runtime view with algorithms and pseudocode, such as handover and You Should Know. Section 7 covers deployment. Section 8 holds cross-cutting concepts that apply across blocks. Section 9 indexes the ADRs. Section 10 holds quality scenarios with numeric measures. Section 11 indexes the risk register, and section 12 is the glossary.

The risk register (risk-register/) lists known agent or product faults, treated as "medical errors" with a cure, in ISO 31000 fields such as likelihood, impact, response and owner. In this material only its index appears, in arc42 section 11.

The reference file, reference/you-should-know-prompt.md, is a verbatim copy of the builtin plugin's prompt. It is named in the layout but its content is not included here.

Every item carries an ID prefix (REQ, OUT, CON, CTX, STR, BB, RT, DEP, CC, QS, TERM, RISK, ADR) and a Source line, so each claim can be traced to a probe, a transcript line, a baseline file, or a user decision.

I can't give you the register's own list. The original material was compacted out of my context, and what I kept is the summary, which notes that only the risk register's index (arc42 section 11) was present and does not record its entries. I won't invent RISK IDs, ratings or owners. What I can offer are risks that the retained decisions and constraints clearly guard against, so treat them as my inference from those rules and check them against section 11 before relying on them.

The first is context loss or a failed renewal in the handover design. Handover replaces core auto compaction through the `session.compact` hook and renews at task boundaries above about 70k tokens (ADR-0178), so if the hook misfires or the boundary is missed, a long session either degrades or loses state with no built-in fallback.

The second is shipping components that don't pay for themselves. ADR-0177 only allows a component when it beats vanilla on a measured check, which suggests the danger is added prompt weight, cost and behavior drift with no measurable benefit.

The third is eval integrity. The constraints section covers it and ADR-0087 (refined by ADR-0180) rules out benchmarks and planner or component swaps, so the risk is a rebuild that appears to pass because the checks were tuned or substituted rather than because it works.

The fourth is cost and model misuse. The rules that Fable and Opus are never a subagent model and that the advisor tool stays disabled point to uncontrolled spend if delegation picks an expensive model.

The fifth is drift from the pinned baseline. The rebuild targets Claude Code 2.1.327 from baseline commit `088a227c`, and the plan leans on measured facts about that version, so hook, tool or settings behavior changing under a newer release could silently invalidate those facts.

The sixth is agent faults that the register frames as "medical errors" with a cure. The bans on a regex Stop check (ADR-0104) and on a constraint ledger (ADR-0075) look like responses to past failure modes, but I can't say which RISK entries they map to without the index.

If you paste section 11 or the register again, I can rank the actual entries and cite their IDs.

END-OF-REPLY

Next, build the foundations in the order the PRD blocks suggest. Begin with the kernel block, because the others depend on it, and read its requirements along with section 5 (what exists at baseline) and section 6 (runtime algorithms). Finally, run the verification block's checks against each plugin (`claudetto`, `claudetto-openspec`, `claudetto-you-should-know`) and compare the results to the baseline before calling a block done.

The risk-register files are only indexed in this material, so these come from risks named in the ADRs, constraints, and context items.

The first is cost from cache breaks. In the user's 2.1.327 sessions, 99 of 104 main-loop cache breaks followed an auto compaction, and about 20.7% of main-loop cache writes re-created content already written. A related fault is the cache breakpoint burst: runs of 22 or more system-reminder blocks, such as a first read loading many path-scoped rules, rebuilt the cache in 43 of 44 steps past 25 positions. ADR-0136 and ADR-0178 exist to contain this.

The second is silent loss of the handover. The `session.compact` hook only accepts one return shape, `{role:"user", text, toolUses:[]}`. A wrong shape is logged and skipped, so core runs its own summarizer, costs an extra request, and drops the handover (CTX-843, ADR-0184). Only one plugin's `session.compact` answer wins, so a second plugin or the old installed copy can also override it. Under `-p`, a mod cannot clear or compact the session at all.

The third is sycophancy and over-correction. CAVE-Bench found agents reverting correct work after false accusations in 12.5% of Sonnet-5 runs and 19.7% of Opus-5 runs, and accusations placed in project files or subagent reports were acted on in roughly 37 to 40% of runs. ADR-0181 answers with an evidence-before-reversal rule, but its effect on the 5.5 models is unmeasured and it must not turn into refusal.

The fourth is security under a minimal sandbox. ADR-0188 turns on auto-allow for sandboxed commands to cut friction, which means an injected command runs with no human check. It can read anything outside `denyRead` and, with all domains allowed, send it out. The sandbox only prevents persistence, so exfiltration has to be handled by breaking the lethal trifecta. Related limits include MCP servers not being sandboxed and Jev being barred from ever answering allow because it is not hardened against injection.

The fifth is irreversible data loss from the automatic disk collector in ADR-0185. A removed Docker volume cannot be recovered, and a database volume idle for seven days could be lost. The unattached-for-seven-days rule and keeping containers bound the risk, but they do not remove it.

The sixth is that builtin disabling does not fully hold. A plugin cannot refuse a builtin, and a settings write removes skills and commands but leaves the builtin's hooks module running until `/reload-plugins` or restart (ADR-0057). Session-start repair of drift covers this, but the window after a write remains.

The last is guard friction and false denials. Earlier gates produced 132 denials with at least 8 false, path spam, and the agent switching the sandbox off on tens of thousands of Bash calls. A guard that blocks routine work trains the agent around it, which is why many were removed.

One session set `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` on 21,504 calls after two real blocks, which means the sandbox then protected nothing and, in auto mode, cost a classifier review on each call. A related hazard is that rewriting a tool call's input voids auto mode's server review, so calls return "gave no verdict".

The third is data loss from automatic cleanup. ADR-0185 has claudetto collect garbage across the system without asking. It names the strongest risk itself: a removed Docker volume is unrecoverable, so a database volume idle for 7 days could vanish. The material also reports a real 10 GB folder lost on a worktree merge, which is why the staging guards are required.

The fourth is that a plugin cannot reliably enforce its own disables. A plugin cannot refuse a `@builtin` at runtime. Rewriting user settings removes skills and commands about 1.2 to 1.5 seconds later, but a builtin's hooks module keeps running until `/reload-plugins` or a restart, and a `Skill` call right after the write can still launch. The headless case is worse, since `/reload-plugins` refuses there.

The fifth is fragile handover. `session.compact` accepts only the exact shape `{role:"user", text, toolUses:[]}`. A wrong shape silently falls back to the default summary and costs a summarizer call while losing the handover (RISK-489). Only one plugin's `session.compact` answer wins, so handover must live in a single module. Under `-p` the mod cannot clear the session at all, so the driver script has to send the clear.

The sixth is agent behavior faults. CAVE-Bench reports models reversing correct work under false accusation, with over-correction in 12.5% of Sonnet-5 runs and 19.7% of Opus-5 runs, and in 39.7% of runs when the accusation sits in project files. The material also records sycophantic openers, false completion, acting on guesses, and eval gaming, where graders or scaffolds are edited after a run is seen. Those are treated as "medical errors" needing a general cure, and the numbers come from preprints on older models, so the effect on claudetto is unmeasured until the ADR-0177 test runs.

The seventh is the evidence base itself. Many facts were measured on 2.1.325 or 2.1.326, minified chunk names and offsets shift between versions, and 145 items kept a source the audit could not find. Thirteen items were removed for lacking any source, and several cited session logs are no longer on disk. A stale fact could therefore drive a wrong design decision.
